summary.title: Faster Networks + Cheaper Messages => Microservices => Functions => Edge
summary.one_liner: Adrian Cockcroft's microXchg 2017 talk argues that faster networks and cheaper messaging drove the move from monoliths to microservices and now to functions, with Lambda code pushed to edge locations.
takeaways: Cheaper, faster messaging (faster networks plus binary formats like Avro and gRPC instead of XML) made it practical to split systems into many microservices and then into functions.
Deployment has evolved from manual releases to automated immutable blue-green deploys, containers, and pay-per-use serverless functions that start in milliseconds.
Serverless is progressing from function hosting to event-driven infrastructure and then to functions running at CDN edge locations, close to customers.
Edge functions face a tension: they lose low-latency access to datacenter services, which may favor more monolithic cores with fewer messages.
Organizational structure matters: use inverse Conway maneuver, small cross-functional teams that own services end to end, and high-trust teams to avoid a distributed monolith.
summary.summary: This is a blog post by High Scalability summarizing Adrian Cockcroft's microXchg 2017 talk, "Shrinking Microservices to Functions." It traces architecture history from monoliths and XML web services to microservices, containers, and Lambda-style serverless, attributing each step to network and messaging improvements. It then covers the next phase, Lambda functions at CDN edge locations with Greengrass and Snowball Edge, and notes the open latency tension this raises. The post closes with organizational advice on team structure and a brief note on AWS lock-in. The page itself is a gloss of the talk and gives no benchmarks beyond the figures the speaker cites.
